prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B018) first. The principle is clean and was proposed before it was realised: a magic-wavelength lattice makes the light shift of the clock transition cancel, so many atoms can be held without Doppler or recoil broadening. The result is measured, not inferred, with fractional uncertainty and stability near 1e-18 that has been confirmed in several independent laboratories and compared between clocks. Four of the six members who ranked it put it first, and nobody argues against its originality. The consequences are concrete and still growing: the coming redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of constant variation and searches for ultralight dark matter. The attribution is also among the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking the lattice clock to its accuracy and many-body limits. Maturity is not in doubt after more than twenty years of independent confirmation. A single-part, two-person prize is therefore a complete, defensible configuration and does not need a second part to be balanced.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a committee could read lattice clocks as the sum of earlier recognised steps: laser cooling (1997), the optical frequency comb (2005) and ion control and ion clocks (2012). On that reading the lattice step looks like a refinement of already-honoured work. Related to that, the redefinition of the second has not yet been adopted, so the headline application is still pending, and the field has competing clock lineages (single-ion clocks, and groups in Paris and elsewhere) that a two-name prize leaves outside. I do not find this decisive, because the magic-wavelength idea is a new concept that changes what is possible, but a prize built on measurement precision could also be seen as metrology rather than a discovery in physics.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B007) first as a new instrument that opened neutrino astronomy and addressed the origin of cosmic rays, prefers a two-person Halzen-Karle prize over adding Yoshida, and ranks lattice clocks only fifth.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube is a serious candidate and the instrument was a real achievement, which is why B007 is one of my alternatives. Two points keep me from putting it first. The attribution is harder than the clean two-name framing suggests: it is a collaboration of hundreds, the credited list has three names, and cutting to Halzen and Karle excludes Yoshida, who is credited in the nomination, and the AMANDA lineage. Second, the source-identification evidence (TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane) is real but still thin compared with the metrological record of the clocks, where independent groups compare at 1e-18. The diffuse flux is the settled result; the source astronomy is not yet mature. I would like to hear what Pearce thinks settles the Karle and Yoshida question, since that decides whether B007 is a two-name or three-name prize.

responses.point: Johansson ranks Cirac-Zoller (B032) first: the 1995 ion-gate proposal and the later cold-atom and Rydberg proposals gave quantum computation and simulation a concrete architecture, with a clean two-person credit; he places lattice clocks seventh.
responses.response: The Cirac-Zoller proposals are original and I would not be unhappy to see them recognised, so B032 is an alternative of mine. My qualification is about what is being rewarded. The trapped-ion gate was realised by others, and that experimental credit is partly covered by the 2012 prize, so honouring only the theorists asks the committee to reward a blueprint whose realisation was credited elsewhere, and whose payoff in scalable quantum computing is still open. The clocks are a demonstrated instrument with a measured result. I also note that Johansson's ballot calls Ye's overlap with other candidates a minor point and gives clocks a high importance, so I would like to know what pushed them down to seventh; if it is the earlier recognition of cooling and combs, that is the same concern I raise in my own case against.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B002) first, as exact, general statements about work and entropy production in small systems, with Evans, Jarzynski and Seifert as three distinct decisive steps and Crooks with a strong claim.
responses.response: I accept that fluctuation theorems are conceptually clean and have become a working language in colloids and single-molecule experiments, and I would not dismiss the candidate. My difficulty is attribution. Mehlig himself names four credible people and proposes three, and the nomination lists Crooks too, so any prize leaves out someone whose claim he calls strong. The field also consists of several results (steady-state fluctuation relation, Jarzynski equality, trajectory-level thermodynamics) that are better described as a framework than as one achievement. That does not make B002 unworthy, but it is harder to give a short, accurate citation than for lattice clocks, and only one member put it first with no other member ranking it.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks lattice clocks first but raises whether the committee should credit the broader optical-clock lineage, including ion clocks, rather than the lattice step alone, and notes she cannot verify the priority history.
responses.response: I take the lineage question seriously and it is the same as the first half of my case against. My view is that the lattice-clock step is separable and citable on its own: the magic-wavelength lattice is what allows large atom numbers with negligible light shift, which is why stability reached the 1e-18 regime quickly. Ion clocks reached comparable uncertainty by a different route and are in a different tradition, partly recognised in 2012. I would keep the citation specific to lattice clocks and magic-wavelength trapping, and I accept that it may be worth a sentence in the citation about the earlier cooling and comb work. On priority I agree it is worth checking, but both of the credited people, Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for accuracy, are consistently described the same way across the ballots.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as a distinct achievement or as the application of cooling (1997), combs (2005) and ion control (2012).

Whether the precise priority between the early lattice proposals and the first clock operation, and the roles of other lattice-clock groups, is as clear as the ballots suggest; I have not verified it independently.
How much weight a measurement-precision achievement should get when the redefinition of the second is still pending.
Whether the attribution and maturity concerns for IceCube (B007) can be resolved to a clean two- or three-name prize, since that is the main competitor for first place.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye. A distant one should be on the record: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and colleagues' ballots mention Hall's laser-stabilisation and comb work as background to the clocks, though Hall is not a credited name. Separately, I take part in WACQT management and have worked in quantum information at Lund, so I would stay out of any deciding discussion on circuit QED (B008), which is why I have not listed it as an alternative even though I ranked it second in the opening round. No specific conflict is apparent for B018, B007 or B032 from the provided profile.
